courses.title: Kasi Shop Compliance Essentials
courses.summary: A short, plain-language course covering what every township shop owner needs to trade legally — registration, food safety, and by-laws.
courses.issuedWith: Dept. of Small Business Development pilot programme

lessons.title: Getting registered
body: Every trading business needs to be registered with the Companies and Intellectual Property Commission (CIPC), and with SARS for tax purposes. If you employ anyone, you also need to register for UIF.
Registration is what makes a pool, an exchange trade, or a customer order enforceable — it's what turns a stall into a business the law (and this platform) recognises.
Municipalities also require spaza shops and food handling outlets to register locally, following the national registration drive that began in late 2024.

lessons.title: Food safety and the Certificate of Acceptability
body: If you sell any food — packaged or prepared — your premises need a Certificate of Acceptability (CoA) from your municipality's Environmental Health Department, under Regulation R638.
This covers safe storage temperatures, pest control, clean surfaces, and separating raw and cooked food.
Operating without a CoA is a criminal offence, and non-compliant premises can be closed immediately by inspectors — this isn't optional paperwork.

lessons.title: Municipal by-laws and trading permits
body: Beyond national registration, your local municipality may require a trading licence or permit for the specific location you trade from.
Keep proof of address and, where relevant, your landlord or property owner's consent — inspectors and verifiers will ask for these alongside your CIPC and CoA documents.

lessons.title: Why this matters for you on MzansiConnect
body: Only verified shops appear on the customer map, can post or respond to exchange listings, and can join bulk-buying pools.
This protects customers, and it protects you — a verified badge is what lets other shop owners trust you enough to trade stock with you.
Every new shop must pass this quiz to register. Passing issues your certificate and makes your shop Verified straight away.

quiz.question: Which three bodies must most trading businesses register with?
options: CIPC, SARS, and UIF (if you employ staff)
Only your local municipality
Only the bank you use
Facebook Business and Google Maps

quiz.question: What does a Certificate of Acceptability cover?
options: Your business's tax rate
Food safety and hygiene at your premises, under Regulation R638
Your eligibility for a bank loan
Your shop's insurance policy

quiz.question: What can happen if your premises don't meet food safety regulations?
options: Nothing, as long as you're registered with CIPC
You get a warning letter after a year
Inspectors can close the premises immediately
You lose your CIPC registration only

quiz.question: Why does MzansiConnect require shops to be verified?
options: To charge higher fees to verified shops
So only compliant shops appear to customers and can trade with other shops
Verification is just cosmetic and has no effect on features
To limit the number of shops on the platform

quiz.question: Can you register a shop on MzansiConnect without passing this quiz?
options: Yes — the quiz is optional
Yes, if a customer vouches for you
No — every shop must pass it to register
Only if you register on a weekend

funding.name: Spaza Shop Support Fund
funding.provider: Dept. of Small Business Development · NEF & SEDFA
funding.amountText: Up to R100 000 (more for registered, compliant shops)
funding.summary: The national R500 million fund for South African-owned spaza shops and food outlets in townships and rural areas: stock, equipment, point-of-sale and training.
offers: Stock grant of up to R40 000, bought through approved wholesale partners
Equipment and shop upgrades — fridges, shelving, security, POS devices
Training in business skills, food safety, compliance and digital payments
Access to bulk purchasing through wholesale aggregation
eligibility: Owner is a South African citizen who runs the shop day to day
Shop is in a township or rural area and serves the local community
Registered with the municipality (trading licence or permit)
Meets food safety and health standards
CIPC registration needed within six months for larger amounts
funding.priority: Youth (18–35), women-owned shops and owners with disabilities get priority.
howToApply: Get your municipal trading permit first — it is the most common reason applications fail.
Apply through the National Empowerment Fund or SEDFA online portals.
Have your ID, proof of address and permit ready to upload.

funding.name: Township and Rural Entrepreneurship Programme (TREP)
funding.provider: Dept. of Small Business Development · SEDFA
funding.summary: Blended finance and business support for enterprises based in townships and rural areas, owned by people who live there.
offers: Finance for stock, equipment and working capital
Business development support alongside the funding
eligibility: South African owner living in the township or rural area
Business operates in that township or rural area
CIPC documents and proof of address available
Quotations attached for any equipment requested
howToApply: Register on the government SMME portal and keep the reference number.
Create a profile on eservices.gov.za with the same email address.
Choose “apply for finance”, fill in the common application and upload CIPC documents and proof of address.

funding.name: NYDA Grant Programme
funding.summary: Grant funding for 100% youth-owned businesses, paid to suppliers for equipment and stock, with mentorship attached.
offers: Grant for equipment, tools and stock (paid directly to suppliers)
eligibility: Every owner is 18–35 and a South African citizen or permanent resident
You work in the business full time
Turnover is under the NYDA limit
Willing to complete NYDA training and accept a mentor
howToApply: Register on the NYDA online portal and choose the Grant Programme.
Upload your ID, business plan, supplier quotes and bank confirmation letter.
Expect a phone or in-person pitch before the committee decides.

funding.name: Tholoana Enterprise Programme
funding.summary: An 18-month programme for established black-owned businesses ready to grow: diagnostics, dedicated mentors and market access. Township businesses get priority consideration.
offers: A structured diagnostic of you and your business
Help with finance, operations and getting into bigger markets
eligibility: At least 51% black-owned and managed, registered in South Africa
Trading consistently for at least two years
Recurring revenue and repeat customers you can show
funding.priority: Women, youth, people with disabilities and township/rural businesses.
howToApply: Apply online on the SAB Foundation website before the closing date.

funding.name: Spaza Shop Training & Support (W&R SETA with SEDFA)
funding.amountText: Free training, with starter stock for some participants
funding.summary: In-person training for spaza owners on inventory management, compliance and point-of-sale, run with SEDFA. Some cohorts receive stock or equipment support afterwards.
offers: Starter stock or POS equipment for selected participants
eligibility: Licence to trade or municipal permit
howToApply: Register for a session on the Training page in MzansiConnect, or contact your nearest SEDFA office.
